displayPassage: Allan Houser created contemporary Apache sculpture. As a child, he listened to his father's stories about the adventures of Chief Geronimo. This gave him a deep __(a) attachment__ to his ancestral background, an attachment that is shown in his artwork. Houser studied at the Indian School in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and then __(b) remained__ in Santa Fe, where he worked as a freelance artist. During World War II, he traveled to California, where he became interested in the media of sculpture. He created works in a variety of styles and mastered bronze, metal, and stone sculpture. Houser's designs are modern, yet firmly __(c) rooted__ in the special tradition of his Native American forefathers. He drew inspiration from both past and present, but like all successful artists, his sculpture __(d) binds__ race and language. The sculpture Reverie shows a distinct Native American influence, but it can be __(e) appreciated__ by anyone, regardless of his or her background.

wrongOptionExplanations.②: 산타페에서 공부한 뒤 그곳에 '남아서' 프리랜서 예술가로 일했다는 문맥이므로 적절합니다.

displayPassage: We tend to think of technology as shiny tools and gadgets. Even if we acknowledge that technology can exist in disembodied form, such as software, we tend not to __(a) incorporate__ in this category paintings, literature, music, dance, poetry, and the arts in general. But we should. If a thousand lines of letters in UNIX __(b) functions__ as a technology (the computer code for a web page), then a thousand lines of letters in English (Hamlet) must qualify as well. They both can change our behavior, alter the course of events, or enable future inventions. A Shakespeare sonnet and a Schubert symphony, then, are in the same category as Google's search engine and the smartphone: They are something __(c) valuable__ produced by a mind. We can't __(d) distinguish__ out the multiple overlapping technologies responsible for a Lord of the Rings movie. The literary rendering of the original novel is as much an __(e) illusion__ as the digital rendering of its fantastical creatures. Both are useful works of the human imagination. Both influence audiences powerfully. Both are technological.

wrongOptionExplanations.②: 컴퓨터 코드가 기술로서 기능한다면 문학도 그러해야 한다는 논리이므로 functions(기능하다/자격을 얻다)는 적절합니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.③: 기술과 예술 모두 정신이 만들어낸 유용하고 가치 있는 것이라는 의미이므로 valuable(가치 있는)은 적절합니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.④: 영화 제작에 관여된 여러 겹치는 기술들을 명확히 떼어놓을 수 없다는 의미이므로 distinguish(구별하다, 분리하다)는 적절합니다.

displayPassage: We all enjoy the pleasure of being left alone with a good book. But sometimes after several hours of immersion we lift our heads and look around, suddenly struck by the quiet, the __(a) absence__ of others. In this situation, we are __(b) suffering__ from reading-induced loneliness. The solution is to read in the company of other people who are reading - whether in a public space such as a café or a library, or in your own home, with your reading friend or partner at the other end of the sofa. Next time you look up, you'll see someone else similarly __(c) immersed__, and you won't feel alone at all. Reading can be __(d) isolated__. Consider joining a reading group in which everybody takes turns reading aloud from a novel. Reading a book collaboratively is a wonderful way to __(e) share__ an otherwise internal and solitary experience.

displayPassage: The human brain is wired to look for threats - a trait that kept us alive when we were living on the savannas but that can __(a) prevent__ happiness in our modern lives. This so-called "negativity bias" can keep you focused on what's going __(b) wrong__ (which explains why complaining is such a popular pastime). To break out of this neural rut, train yourself to __(c) acknowledge__ when things go right. If you keep a calendar or a journal, make a point to write down what went well. If you're more of a verbal processor, start your conversations with friends by __(d) concealing__ a recent win (anything that gives you that yesssss feeling). Where the mind goes, reality follows. The more you __(e) appreciate__ life, the more reasons you have to celebrate it.

displayPassage: When we see something, we naturally and automatically break it up into shapes, colors, and concepts that we have learned through education. We recode what we see through the lens of everything we know. We __(a) reconstruct__ memories rather than retrieving the video from memory. This is a useful trait. It's a more __(b) efficient__ way to store information - a bit like an optimal image compression algorithm such as JPG, rather than storing a raw bitmap image file. People who lack this ability and remember everything in perfect detail __(c) struggle__ to generalize, learn, and make connections between what they have learned. But representing the world as abstract ideas and features comes at a __(d) benefit__ of seeing the world as it is. Instead, we see the world through our assumptions, motivations, and past experiences. The discovery that our memories are reconstructed through abstract representations rather than played back like a movie completely __(e) undermined__ the legal primacy of eyewitness testimony. Seeing is not believing.

wrongOptionExplanations.⑤: 기억이 변형된 채 재구성된다는 점 때문에 목격자 증언의 법적 우위가 약화되는 것은 자연스러운 논리 연결입니다.
